title: “Guard Against” Advice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post describes a form of coaching advice in which a leader asks a team member to "guard against" a potential problem that has not yet materialized. When offered out of a genuine desire to help, such mild warnings can prevent trouble before it becomes serious. The author cautions that without a caring tone the advice reads as criticism of an existing problem, and too much of it can erode confidence and make people mechanical. Even so, many leaders withhold such cautions and rob their people of experience and foresight; the post argues good leaders speak up and are wise rather than alarmist.
points: Preventive warnings address issues that are not yet significant and so differ from feedback on existing problems.
The advice only works when it clearly comes from a desire to help.
Overuse can undermine confidence and make people inauthentic.
Withholding foresight deprives team members of the leader's experience.
quotes: Good leaders anticipate the challenges and issues faced by team members and move to prevent them from becoming problems.

They provide invaluable advice when they offer a caution or warning about a potential quagmire. When given in a caring and positive way, these “guard against” messages can avert an unfolding issue or thwart an unseen roadblock.
To be effective, this mild warning must come from a desire to help, or it will be viewed as feedback about a problem that already exists.
Too much “guard against” advice can undermine the confidence of a team member and make them overly mechanical or inauthentic in their approach to issues.

When good leaders see a potential problem that has yet to materialize, they don’t keep their premonition to themselves. In their desire to help team members sidestep a likely difficulty, they find a way to suggest a cautionary approach.
